summary: Measured in a review tree (copy of the staged index), 14 mutations built and run against :format:test, :sequencer:test, :ingest:test. THE FORMAT LAYER IS STRONG AND EVERY HEADLINE MUTATION DIES. (1) The PARTIAL HOIST -- podId per segment, incarnation+flushSeq once per delta and fanned out on decode -- is killed three times: AttributedDeltaTest#everySegmentKeepsItsOwnTripleAcrossABatch, GoldenAttributedTest#anAttributedDeltaFromAnEarlierBuildStillParses and #reEncodingTheAttributedDeltaReproducesItByteForByte. The goldens' differing flushSeq (4/5/0) is the killer and it works: I confirmed the sequencer suite alone survives that mutation, so the format fixtures are carrying it, not CommitLogAttributionTest (whose store round-trip is single-segment). (2) THE MINTING SITE: moving the mint into flushLocked fails IngestCommitPathTest#theIncarnationIsMintedOncePerIngestInstanceAndDiffersBetweenTwoOfThem and nothing else in :ingest:test -- and appendOnce() calls flushNow(), so the two-flush half is not vacuous; a `private static final` incarnation (one per process, not per instance) also dies there. (3) THE LEGACY FREEZE: forcing the attributed shape kills GoldenAttributedTest#theLegacyGoldensAreUnchangedByThisChange plus GoldenCheckpointTest, AttributedDeltaTest#aDeltaWithNoAttributionEncodesExactlyAsBefore, BatchedCommitDeltaTest (4 methods) and GoldenChainEntryTest (3). (4) Dropping the attribution in CommitLog.commitAll kills both CommitLogAttributionTest methods; ignoring the attributed pod slot on decode kills both new CheckpointPodStateTest methods and two GoldenAttributedTest ones. RED RECORDS ARE HONEST: all 12 new methods carry records dated 09-06/09-07 in .harness/tdd/red.json, and I observed each new method green with the code and red under a mutation of ITS OWN behaviour (the two exceptions -- theDeltaGoldenUsesTheReservedKind..., aV0CheckpointStillDecodes... -- are structural byte/version assertions whose subject cannot be mutated without dying elsewhere first). WHAT IS NOT COVERED IS EVERYTHING THIS COMMIT ADDED OUTSIDE THE TWO WIRE LAYOUTS. Five new production behaviours survive deletion or replacement with a constant: the incarnation-aware merge in CheckpointWriter (the pre-ADR Math::max is still green), the pointer's VALUE (0/0 constant is green; the value actually written is measured to be nextSequence, i.e. one past the delta that applied), the enumerated version set (`version > VERSION_ATTRIBUTED` is green, and the new comment asserting otherwise is false), PodState's three invariants (all deletable, green) and CommitRequest's incarnationId guard (deletable, green). Four of the five are one fixture or one assertLine each.

findings.summary: The incarnation-aware merge -- the one production behaviour ADR-0036 exists to make possible -- is entirely unconstrained. Every CheckpointWriter fixture in the tree passes the literal incarnation "i1" (CheckpointWriterContentTest:60, CheckpointWriterTriggerTest:97,230,242-245, CheckpointDiscoveryTest:406, LocalSequencerCheckpointTest:85,90), so no test ever presents two incarnations of one pod. #aPodsFlushSeqNeverGoesBACKWARDSWhenAnOlderFlushArrivesLate is depth-one within a single incarnation and passes either way. The row's own notes predicted this ("the Math::max-over-bare-podId test whose premise inverts. Budget for that rather than discovering it"): the assertion was rewritten for the new type but not extended to the new branch.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: replacing the merge lambda at CheckpointWriter.java:138-141 with the pre-ADR-0036 body `(existing, incoming) -> existing.lastAppliedFlushSeq() > incoming.lastAppliedFlushSeq() ? existing : incoming` -- i.e. carrying Math::max ACROSS incarnations -- leaves :sequencer:test and :ingest:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. I drove the real CommitLog+CheckpointWriter with poda/i1/flushSeq=9, then poda/i2/flushSeq=0, then poda/i2/flushSeq=1: the staged code writes PodState[i2, 1, ...] and the mutant writes PodState[i1, 9, ...]. Under the mutant, M4.10d suppresses a restarted pod's second commit for ever and records the DEAD incarnation's id in the checkpoint -- the exact suppression ADR-0036 exists to prevent -- with the suite green. Depth two is what is needed and a depth-one fixture (restart then one commit) also passes the mutant, since `incoming` wins on the first restarted commit either way.
findings.remedy: One test in CheckpointWriterContentTest: commit(poda,"i1",9), then commit(poda,"i2",0), then commit(poda,"i2",1), and assert the slot is PodState with incarnationId "i2" and lastAppliedFlushSeq 1 -- not 9 and not "i1".

findings.summary: The POINTER's value is never asserted anywhere -- only `hasPointer()).isTrue()` and `incarnationId()).isNotNull()`, both of which are functions of incarnationId alone (Checkpoint.java:91-93), not of epoch/sequence. Checkpoint.PodState's javadoc calls the pointer "WHAT MAKES A REPLAY ANSWERABLE" and M4.10d will GET the pointed delta, so the address is the payload of this row's checkpoint change, and no test can tell a right address from a wrong one. Same gap in CheckpointDiscoveryTest:406-410 and LocalSequencerCheckpointTest:100-104.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: replacing CheckpointWriter.java:125-126 with `long pointerEpoch = 0; long pointerSequence = 0;` leaves :sequencer:test and :ingest:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL -- a return-a-constant mutation on the field the row exists to add. Swapping the two arguments at the PodState construction site would survive for the same reason. This is not hypothetical: I instrumented the unmutated code and the pointer stored for a delta at sequence 2 is epoch=1, sequence=3, i.e. log.nextSequence() -- one PAST the delta that applied, addressing a slot that does not exist yet and will later hold a different pod's delta. Whether that off-by-one is intended is the production reviewer's call; my point is that no test in the tree would notice either way, so M4.10d will inherit whatever address happens to be there and its own tests will be written to agree with it.
findings.remedy: In CheckpointWriterContentTest, keep the CommitDelta returned by log.commitAll and assert the slot's epoch and sequence against that delta's own (epoch, sequence) -- whichever convention the production reviewer settles on, pin it here.

findings.summary: The added pairing claims to hold the ENUMERATED version set and does not. Its comment says "`version <= VERSION_ATTRIBUTED` would pass the first assertion and fail this pairing's whole point", but the first assertion sets bytes[7]=9 and 9 is not <= 1, so a range check refuses it identically. The second half (a v1 header over a v0 body) exercises the body's version-dependent branch -- which is real and worth having, it dies if decodeBody ignores the version -- but says nothing about enumeration vs range. CheckpointPodStateTest:63-87 repeats the claim in its javadoc ("AN ENUMERATED SET, NEVER `version <= VERSION`") and uses the same non-discriminating v9 byte. The row makes this an acceptance criterion in so many words: "decoded from an ENUMERATED {0,1}" -- testing.md rule 13.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: replacing Checkpoint.java:231 with `if (version > VERSION_ATTRIBUTED)` -- the exact mutation the production comment forbids -- leaves :format:test and :sequencer:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Every version int a writer can emit is 0 or 1, and every value either check rejects is rejected by both, EXCEPT a negative one: corrupt or hostile bytes with the header's high bit set (e.g. bytes[4]=0xFF) give version=-1, which the range mutant accepts and then decodes with v0's layout, while the staged code refuses it by name. When VERSION 2 lands, the mutant silently decodes a v2 body as v1 -- the guess this file's own class comment says it exists to forbid, and the guard whose deletion it records as having left the whole build green.
findings.remedy: Add a negative version to the refusal test (write 0xFF into bytes[4] and assert "unsupported checkpoint version"); that single case kills the range form. Then correct or delete the two comments that claim the v9 byte does it.

findings.summary: PodState's three new invariants have no test: the pointer-both-or-neither rule, the incarnation-and-pointer-travel-together rule, and the non-blank incarnation rule (Checkpoint.java:66-85). This is a decode path for untrusted bytes -- Checkpoint.decode:246-249 deliberately converts the record's IllegalArgumentException into an IOException, and CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest exists to hold exactly that conversion for every OTHER field (wide length, negative count, repeated pod, torn object). The new fields got the guard and no case. testing.md rule 14.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: deleting all three checks from the PodState compact constructor (leaving only the negative-watermark check) leaves :format:test and :sequencer:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. With them gone, a crafted v1 checkpoint whose pod slot sets the flag byte to 1 and then a zero-length incarnationId decodes into PodState["", w, e, s] -- a blank incarnation, which is precisely the identity collapse CommitRequest.java:44-52 refuses at the other end of the same seam -- and a slot whose wire epoch is a 10-byte varint -1 with a real incarnation decodes into a half-pointer that M4.10d will GET. Both are IOException today and neither is asserted, so the conversion can be lost without any test failing.
findings.remedy: Three assertThatThrownBy cases on the record, plus one crafted-bytes case through Checkpoint.decode asserting IOException rather than IllegalArgumentException (the pattern CheckpointDecodeRefusalTest already uses).

findings.summary: CommitRequest's new incarnationId validation is unconstrained in the one file that tests every sibling field's refusal: blank podId (:33), dashed/slashed podId (:45), negative flushSeq (:59), blank segmentKey (:66), empty recordCounts (:73). The commit adds a requireNonNull AND a blank check for incarnationId with a four-line comment explaining that a blank one "collapses every incarnation of a pod into one identity", and adds no case. Every touched line in this file is a mechanical `"i1"` insertion. testing.md rules 13 and 14.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: deleting `Objects.requireNonNull(incarnationId, ...)` and the isBlank throw from CommitRequest.java:44-52 leaves :sequencer:test and :ingest:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Nothing constructs a CommitRequest with a null or blank incarnation, so the guard can be removed or written as `if (incarnationId == null)` (dropping blank) and no test notices; a caller that passes "" -- the natural value from an unset env var or an un-migrated M5 forwarder -- then reaches CommitLog.commitAll:288 and the delta carries a blank incarnation for every segment, making every incarnation of that pod one identity again.
findings.remedy: Two lines beside #aNegativeFlushSeqIsRefused: a null and a "  " incarnationId, asserting NullPointerException and IllegalArgumentException containing "incarnationId".

findings.summary: The fake's javadoc now claims "This fake DOES copy the attribution onto each segment, because a fake that dropped it would let a test pass while the real delta carried nothing for a successor to rebuild from" -- and nothing holds that claim. FakeSequencerTest is touched in 14 places by this commit, all mechanical `"i1"` insertions, and asserts segmentKey, offsets, sequence numbering and per-stream continuation but never attribution. CommitLog's copy IS pinned (CommitLogAttributionTest), so only the fake can drift.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: reverting FakeSequencer:87-89 to the two-argument `new SegmentCommit(request.segmentKey(), runs)` -- the fake silently drops the triple -- leaves :sequencer:test, :ingest:test and :http:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. A future ingest- or client-side test that reads a delta from the fake would then be asserting against a shape the real CommitLog does not produce, which is the divergence the javadoc says it is preventing. Minor because nothing consumes it yet and the real path is pinned; the fix is one assertion.
findings.remedy: One assertion in FakeSequencerTest#theDeltaCarriesTheSegmentKeyItWasCommittedFor (:185): the segment's attribution equals the request's triple.

findings.summary: The -1/-1 sentinel is asserted only through hasPointer()/incarnationId(), never by value, so the distinction the javadoc calls load-bearing -- "epoch and sequence are then -1, NOT zero: (0, 0) is a real delta address, and a slot that looked addressable would answer a replay from the wrong object" -- is unconstrained.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: changing PodState.bare to `new PodState(null, lastAppliedFlushSeq, 0, 0)` with the absent-check changed to `epoch == 0 && sequence == 0` leaves :format:test, :sequencer:test and :ingest:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Every bare slot then carries the address of chain entry (0, 0) -- a real delta -- while hasPointer() still reports false because it keys on incarnationId; a consumer that tests `epoch >= 0` instead (which the constructor's own `pointed` predicate does) reads a v0-recovered pod as addressable and answers a replay from epoch 0 slot 0. Minor because no consumer exists until M4.10d, but the assertion costs one line now and the sentinel is what M4.10d will branch on.
findings.remedy: assertThat(legacy.pods().get("poda").epoch()).isEqualTo(-1) and the same for sequence(), beside the existing incarnationId isNull assertion at :83-85.

findings.summary: The null-value check that replaced the old `p.getValue() == null || p.getValue() < 0` has no test. Its comment justifies why it must stay ("which Map.copyOf would not reach through an unmodifiable view"), and the negative-watermark half of the old check migrated to PodState with its CheckpointTest case intact (:196-198), but the null half is now unconstrained.
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED: deleting `Objects.requireNonNull(p.getValue(), "pod state for " + p.getKey())` leaves :format:test and :sequencer:test BUILD SUCCESSFUL. A HashMap carrying a null PodState then constructs a Checkpoint that throws NullPointerException later, inside encode() at Checkpoint.java:200-201, i.e. on the write path of an already-acknowledged commit instead of at construction.
findings.remedy: One assertThatThrownBy in CheckpointTest#theConstructorRefusesValuesTheWireCanCarry using a HashMap with a null value.
